outcome: Not settled as of 11 October 2026, but the general bound and several special cases moved since 26 January 2024: Aires, Chan, Pak and Panova (arXiv 2609.30888, posted 25 Sep 2026, unrefereed) prove a pair with probability in [(5-sqrt5)/10+eps, (5+sqrt5)/10-eps] for every finite non-chain poset, which is wider than the bullet's [1/3, 2/3] and so does not give it, while their Theorem 1.4 gives the bullet's window for finite posets of width above a universal K; Anish Gupta (arXiv 2607.23926, 27 Jul 2026) verifies the Gold Partition Conjecture, and so the bullet, for all non-chain posets with at most 14 elements; and a claimed proof of the Kahn-Saks conjecture by Max Aires (USC-hosted PDF, 25 Sep 2026, not read by me) would give the window for all posets of sufficiently large width if correct.
problem_asks: The statement asks, for every finite partially ordered set P that is not totally ordered (not a chain): does there exist a pair of elements x, y of P such that the probability that x precedes y in a uniformly random linear extension of P lies in the closed interval [1/3, 2/3]? Unpacked: (1) a universal claim over all finite non-chain posets (the word 'finite' excludes infinite posets, for which the analogous statement is known to fail); (2) for each such P, existence of one pair (x, y) whose probability lies in [1/3, 2/3], with both endpoints counting; equivalently, the balance constant delta(P) = max over pairs of min(P(x<y), P(y<x)) satisfies delta(P) >= 1/3. The statement asks for a pair inside the window [1/3, 2/3] and nothing else: no asymptotic, no width condition, no bound on delta other than 1/3. The constants 1/3 and 2/3 are sharp by the three-element example with one relation (context, not asked).

events.what_happened: J. Kahn and M. Saks, 'Balancing poset extensions', Order 1 (1984) 113-126 (citation taken from the bibliography of arXiv 2509.11549, which I read; the 1984 paper itself was not opened). Proves that every finite non-chain poset has a pair x, y with P(x<y) strictly between 3/11 and 8/11. The same line of work formulated the conjecture that delta(P) tends to 1/2 as the width grows, now called the Kahn-Saks conjecture (Conjecture 1.2 of arXiv 2509.11549).
events.delivers: For every finite non-chain poset, existence of a pair with probability in the open window (3/11, 8/11). That window is wider than [1/3, 2/3], so it does not establish the bullet's window. The width-to-infinity conjecture it states is a different question.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no pair is guaranteed in [1/3, 2/3] for every finite non-chain poset.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal of record; the paper was not read by me

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: it asserts the existence of a balanced pair, with weaker constants.

events.what_happened: N. Linial (1984) is credited, in secondary summaries only, with the width-two case of the bound; M. Aigner (1985) is credited with identifying the extremal width-two posets. Neither original was opened. Sah (arXiv 1811.01500, which I read) describes his own width-two result as extending Linial (1984) and Aigner (1985). The Wikipedia summary I read lists width two among the verified cases citing Linial (1984) and Sah (2021).
events.delivers: Per secondary sources only, the bullet's window for every finite non-chain poset of width two. Not checked against the original.
events.remains: Posets of width three or more.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: G. Brightwell (1989) is credited, in the Wikipedia summary and in Gupta's bibliography, with the conjecture for semiorders. The original was not opened.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources only, the bullet's window for every finite semiorder that is not a chain.
events.remains: Posets that are not semiorders.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: W. T. Trotter, W. G. Gehrlein and P. C. Fishburn, 'Balance theorems for height-2 posets', Order 9 (1992) 43-53; received 1 March 1990, accepted 22 April 1992 (from a search excerpt of the PDF; the PDF was not opened). The excerpt reports Theorem 1 as a strict inequality, which other sources do not reproduce, so the boundary case of the window is unclear to me.
events.delivers: Every finite height-2 poset with at least three points has an incomparable pair with probability in [1/3, 2/3] (strictness at the endpoints uncertain, see what_happened).
events.remains: Posets of height three or more.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper on 22 April 1992 (per search excerpt)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: G. Brightwell, S. Felsner and W. T. Trotter, 'Balancing pairs and the cross product conjecture', Order 12 (1995) 327-349. Proves that every finite non-chain poset has a pair with (5-sqrt5)/10 <= P(x<y) <= (5+sqrt5)/10, about 0.2764 to 0.7236, via a special case of the cross product conjecture. The paper is the source of the statement that this bound is best possible for countably infinite posets (as described in arXiv 2609.30888, which I read). The PDF is scanned and was not machine-readable to me; the bound is taken from arXiv 2609.30888 and from search excerpts.
events.delivers: For every finite non-chain poset, a pair with probability in [(5-sqrt5)/10, (5+sqrt5)/10]. This window is wider than [1/3, 2/3], so it does not establish the bullet. The bound is sharp for infinite posets, which is why the 2026 paper's title refers to an 'infinite barrier'.
events.remains: The bullet's window [1/3, 2/3], i.e. the gap between 0.2764 and 1/3 on the lower side and symmetrically on the upper side, for all finite non-chain posets.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; it gives a weaker window and identifies the infinite-poset obstruction.

events.what_happened: M. Peczarski, 'The Gold Partition Conjecture', Order 23(1) (2006) 89-95. Introduces the Gold Partition Conjecture (GPC), which implies the 1/3-2/3 conjecture and a tight sorting bound, and proves GPC for width-two posets, semiorders and all non-chain posets with at most 11 elements (per search excerpts and the Gupta paper; the original was not opened). The Wikipedia summary also attributes to Peczarski (2006) the result that the proportion of n-element posets satisfying the conjecture tends to 100%.
events.delivers: GPC, a stronger statement, for width-two posets, semiorders, and all non-chain posets with at most 11 elements (finite instances). The asymptotic statement concerns the proportion of posets, not every poset, so it does not settle the bullet.
events.remains: Posets with at least 12 elements outside the width-two and semiorder classes.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; the GPC is a strengthening of it.

events.what_happened: M. Peczarski, 'The Gold Partition Conjecture for 6-thin posets', Order 25 (2008). Proves GPC, and so the bullet, for posets in which every element is incomparable to at most six others (per Gupta's paper and the Wikipedia summary; the original was not opened).
events.delivers: The bullet's window for finite posets in which each element is incomparable to at most six others.
events.remains: Posets with some element incomparable to seven or more elements.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: K. De Loof, B. De Baets and H. De Meyer, 'Counting linear extension majority cycles in partially ordered sets on up to 13 elements' (2010, pp. 1541-1547, per a publication listing; the paper was not opened). An exhaustive enumeration of posets up to 13 elements. Gupta's paper states that it computes the minimum balance constant for each order up to 13 and that orders 12 and 13 match its results.
events.delivers: The bullet's window for all finite non-chain posets with at most 13 elements, as a finite computer census (per Gupta's account; not checked against the paper).
events.remains: Posets with at least 14 elements.

machine_checked.system: Exhaustive computer enumeration (not a proof assistant); details not read

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (finite instances only).

events.what_happened: I. Zaguia, 'The 1/3-2/3 conjecture for N-free ordered sets', arXiv 1107.5626 (posted 28 July 2011); a search excerpt gives the journal version as Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 19(2) (2012) P29. The arXiv listing was opened; the paper was not.
events.delivers: The bullet's window for every finite N-free poset that is not a chain (a class of posets; not all posets).
events.remains: Posets that are not N-free.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: I. Zaguia, 'The 1/3-2/3 Conjecture for ordered sets whose cover graph is a forest', arXiv 1610.00809 (posted 4 Oct 2016; v3 June 2017); Order 36(2) (2019) 335-347 (per search excerpt). The abstract, as read in a search excerpt, proves that every non-total ordered set whose cover graph is a forest has a 'good pair', and that good pairs yield the conjecture.
events.delivers: The bullet's window for finite posets whose cover graph is a forest (a class of posets).
events.remains: Posets whose cover graph is not a forest.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in Order 36(2) (2019) (per search excerpt)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: E. J. Olson and B. E. Sagan, 'On the 1/3-2/3 Conjecture', arXiv 1706.04985 (submitted 15 June 2017; v2 31 Jan 2018); Order (received 21 June 2017, accepted 29 Dec 2017; DOI 10.1007/s11083-017-9450-3). The arXiv abstract was read. It proves the bullet's window for: Boolean, set-partition and subspace lattices; posets arising from Young diagrams (a search excerpt says skew and shifted); and some dimension-2 posets. It also studies posets with a 1/2-balanced pair, for example those with an automorphism having a 2-cycle.
events.delivers: The bullet's window for the listed classes: lattices of the named types, Young-diagram posets, and some dimension-2 posets. These are classes, not all finite posets.
events.remains: All posets outside the listed classes.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper on 29 Dec 2017 (per the DOI record in a search excerpt)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: E. Chen, 'A family of partially ordered sets with small balance constant', arXiv 1709.05753 (posted 18 Sep 2017; revised Oct 2021); Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 25(4) (2018) #P4.43, DOI 10.37236/7337 (per search excerpts; neither the arXiv full text nor the journal page was opened). Constructs posets whose balance constants approach (93-sqrt6697)/32, about 0.3489, answering a question of Brightwell, and notes that it is not known whether balance constants can approach 1/3.
events.revisions: Revised Oct 2021 per search excerpt; journal version EJC 25(4) (2018)
events.delivers: An infinite family of finite posets whose balance constants are all at least about 0.3489 in the limit. This is consistent with the bullet and does not settle it; it says the family does not approach 1/3.
events.remains: The whole bullet, including whether balance constants can approach 1/3.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper as EJC 25(4) #P4.43 (per search excerpt)

events.directly_checkable: The explicit family of posets with balance constants converging to (93-sqrt6697)/32 (the constructions were not read; the limit is from search excerpts and the abstract summary).
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; the family's constants are above 1/3.
events.object: An explicit infinite family of finite posets whose balance constants approach (93-sqrt6697)/32, about 0.3489 (the constructions themselves were not read; the statement is from search excerpts and the arXiv listing).

events.what_happened: A. Sah, 'Improving the 1/3-2/3 conjecture for width two posets', arXiv 1811.01500 (posted 5 Nov 2018; v2 18 June 2021, 'incorporated referee comments'); Combinatorica 41 (2021) 99-126. The arXiv abstract was read. Proves that for width-two posets P that cannot be built from a singleton and the three-element poset with one relation by direct sum, delta(P) >= (-3+5sqrt17)/52, about 0.33876. Also constructs width-two posets T_n with delta(T_n) approaching beta, about 0.348843, which the author says may be optimal.
events.revisions: v2 18 June 2021 (referee comments incorporated); journal version Combinatorica 41 (2021) 99-126
events.delivers: The bullet's window for width-two posets in the stated class, since 0.33876 > 1/3 gives a pair with probability in [0.33876, 0.66124], inside [1/3, 2/3]. The excluded direct-sum class contains the extremal width-two posets, which the Wikipedia summary attributes to Aigner (1985) as attaining 1/3 exactly; this is consistent with, but not shown by, the abstract I read.
events.remains: Posets of width three or more; and the excluded direct-sum class of width-two posets, which is covered only by the older width-two results (Linial/Aigner, per secondary sources).

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal of record; version 2 states referee comments were incorporated
checked_by.what_they_did: Refereed and published the paper in Combinatorica 41 (2021)

events.directly_checkable: The explicit width-two posets T_n with balance constants approaching beta, about 0.348843 (construction not read; the statement is from the abstract).
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; it is the strongest known uniform width-two bound.
events.object: Posets T_n of width two whose balance constants approach beta, about 0.348843 (the constructions were not read; the statement is from the abstract). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: M. Peczarski, 'The worst balanced partially ordered sets - ladders with broken rungs', Experimental Mathematics 28 (2019) 181-184 (citation taken from Gupta's arXiv 2607.23926, which I read; the paper itself was not opened). Gupta reports that Peczarski conjectured that no poset has a balance constant strictly between 1/3 and about 0.348843. The year the conjecture was first stated is not verified; the Wikipedia summary also gives 2019.
events.delivers: A conjectured empty gap in the balance constants between 1/3 and about 0.348843. A conjecture, not a proof of the bullet.
events.remains: The whole bullet.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture, which it does not prove.
events.object: Ladders with broken rungs are named in Gupta's paper as the worst balanced posets among non-trivial ordinal sums (balance constant 254/725 among those up to order 14).

events.what_happened: C. Gaetz and Y. Gao, 'Balance constants for Coxeter groups', arXiv 2005.09719 (posted 19 May 2020, about 28 pages); Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 376 (2023) 8973-9000 (per an author listing); FPSAC 2021 extended abstract, Seminaire Lotharingien de Combinatoire article 41 (per search excerpt). The arXiv listing was read; the abstract and full text were not. They recast balance constants for convex subsets of Coxeter groups and prove the analogous bound for weak-order intervals below fully commutative elements in acyclic Coxeter groups. They conjecture the 1/3 bound for convex subsets of finite Weyl groups (arXiv and FPSAC wording; some talk abstracts say finite Coxeter groups).
events.revisions: Journal version Trans. AMS 376 (2023) per author listing; FPSAC 2021 abstract
events.delivers: An analogue, for convex subsets of Coxeter groups, of the bullet's statement, with proofs for weak-order intervals below fully commutative elements. This is a different family of objects, so it does not establish the bullet for posets.
events.remains: The poset bullet; the Coxeter analogue is not the bullet's question.

checked_by.who: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society (referees)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2023 (per an author listing; not confirmed on the journal site)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the analogue; not a poset result.

events.what_happened: S. H. Chan, I. Pak and G. Panova, 'The cross-product conjecture for width two posets', arXiv 2104.09009 (posted 19 Apr 2021; v3). Proves the cross-product inequality (CPC) of Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter for width-two posets, with two proofs (per search excerpts; not opened). The CPC is the inequality from which BFT derived their 1995 bound.
events.delivers: The cross-product inequality for width-two posets. Sources read do not state that it yields the bullet's window for width two; Sah's bound is the one stated to do that.
events.remains: The CPC for posets of width three or more, and the bullet.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against the bullet directly: it is an inequality in the same circle of ideas.

events.what_happened: S. H. Chan, I. Pak and G. Panova, 'On the cross-product conjecture for the number of linear extensions', arXiv 2306.09240 (submitted 15 June 2023; v1 only; 24 pages; journal reference Can. J. Math. 77 (2025) 535-562). The abstract page was read. It proves a weak version of the cross-product conjecture, with a constant epsilon > 0 depending on the poset, proves the converse inequality, and disproves the generalized cross-product conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 only; journal version Can. J. Math. 77 (2025)
events.delivers: A weak, poset-dependent-constant version of the CPC and the converse inequality; a disproof of a generalized form. It does not give the bullet's window.
events.remains: The CPC itself and the bullet.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published as Can. J. Math. 77 (2025) 535-562 (per arXiv journal reference)

events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against the bullet; it is a related inequality with a weak form proved.

events.what_happened: A. Dolores-Cuenca, J. Guzman-Saenz and S. Kim, 'The gold partition conjecture and the lexicographic sum of posets', arXiv 2410.12494 (October 2024 arXiv identifier; search excerpt only, not opened). Per the excerpt: if a poset Q satisfies the conjecture then so does any lexicographic sum of a poset P with Q placed at a point of P.
events.delivers: A closure statement: from posets Q satisfying the conjecture, lexicographic sums with Q at a point also satisfy it. This produces new families from known ones; it is not a proof for all posets.
events.remains: Posets not generated by this operation from satisfying posets, which includes the general bullet.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: O. Rozinek, 'A Similarity Space Approach to the 1/3-2/3 Conjecture in Partially Ordered Sets', Informatics 2024: 17th IEEE International Scientific Conference on Informatics, pp. 532-537, IEEE (no DOI shown). Read from the author's faculty-site record: it introduces a 'balance constant' within similarity spaces with supremum 1/2, states that the infimum of normalized similarity over posets is 1/3 (the 'main contribution'), and says the approach provides a proof of the 1/3-2/3 conjecture in the general case. The same record carries the author's caveat, verbatim: 'a more rigorous and detailed proof is still needed to fully resolve this longstanding problem'. Related PhD thesis, 'Similarity Space and Its Applications', University of Pardubice, April 2024 (search excerpt).
events.delivers: As claimed in the abstract: that the infimum of normalized similarity over finite posets is 1/3, with the author saying this yields the general conjecture. Whether the similarity quantity is the balance constant delta(P) of linear extensions is not established by anything I could read; the record's own caveat says the general proof is incomplete.
events.remains: The whole bullet, on the author's own caveat; and whether the similarity quantity equals delta(P).
events.doubts: (1) The author's own record says a more rigorous and detailed proof is still needed, which conflicts with the claim of a general proof on the same page. (2) The main quantity is normalized similarity in a similarity-space framework; the record does not show it is the linear-extension balance constant. (3) The full text is not readable to me (IEEE and the Czech repository blocked), so the argument could not be checked. (4) No independent engagement found.
events.direction: Claimed, as stated in the abstract, to support the 1/3 bound; the author's caveat weakens that claim.

events.what_happened: M. Aires and J. Kahn, 'Balancing extensions in posets of large width', arXiv 2509.11549 (submitted 15 Sep 2025; v1 only; 34 KB). The full HTML was read. Proves: delta(P) tends to 1/2 as n = |P| tends to infinity if the width is Omega(n) or there are omega(log n) minimal elements (recovering Komlos's condition |min P| = Omega(n)); delta(P) is at least 1/e - o(1) when the width is omega(sqrt n) or the height is o(n). States the 1/3-2/3 conjecture (Conjecture 1.1) and the Kahn-Saks conjecture (Conjecture 1.2) as open. Their text describes the 1/3-2/3 conjecture as possibly the best known of all poset problems.
events.delivers: Asymptotic statements for large posets in named classes: in each class the bullet's window holds for all sufficiently large n (since 1/e > 1/3 and the limit 1/2 exceeds 1/3). Nothing for small posets or for posets outside these classes.
events.remains: All posets outside the named classes, and all posets below the asymptotic threshold; the bullet in general.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture in the asymptotic, restricted-class sense.

events.what_happened: M. Aires and J. Kahn, 'Variance vs. range for linear extensions, and balancing extensions in posets of bounded width', arXiv 2510.26134 (submitted 30 Oct 2025; v1 only; 11 pages). The abstract page was read; the full text was not. Per the abstract: if the maximum number of elements incomparable to a single element is large, some element has large variance in a random extension; the Kahn-Saks conclusion holds for posets with large variance and bounded width; the authors note a short proof of a result of Chan, Pak and Panova on Young diagrams.
events.delivers: The Kahn-Saks conclusion (delta tends to 1/2) for large posets in the class of bounded width with an element of large incomparability; asymptotic and restricted. Hence the bullet's window for sufficiently large posets in that class.
events.remains: Posets of unbounded width without the variance condition, all small posets, and the bullet in general.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture in a restricted asymptotic sense.

events.what_happened: J. Kahn (Rutgers), joint work with M. Aires, 'Balancing extensions in posets of large width', Harvard-MIT Combinatorics Seminar, 11 May 2026 (announcement page read). The talk abstract restates Conjecture 1 (if P is not a chain then delta(P) >= 1/3) and Conjecture 2 (if w(P) tends to infinity then delta(P) tends to 1/2), and says: 'We are still far from proving either of these, but make some interesting progress.'
events.delivers: No new result; a status statement by the authors in May 2026 that the 1/3 conjecture was not close to proof.
events.remains: The whole bullet.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against; a status statement.

events.what_happened: A. Gupta, 'Balance Constants, Majority Cycles, and the Gold Partition Conjecture through Fourteen Elements', arXiv 2607.23926 (v1 Mon 27 Jul 2026; v2 Thu 30 Jul 2026). Both the abstract page and the HTML were read. Computes exact extremal balance data for all 1,338,193,159,771 unlabeled posets on 14 elements. Theorem 5: every non-chain poset on at most 14 elements satisfies the Gold Partition Conjecture; Corollary 6: every non-chain poset on at most 14 elements has balance constant at least 1/3. Reports that exactly 128 classes attain 1/3, each an ordinal sum of singletons and copies of one three-element poset; that the least balance constant above 1/3 is 37/106; that the least among posets that are not nontrivial ordinal sums is 254/725, attained by a ladder with broken rungs; and that the longest simple cycle in the majority digraph has length 8 (30 classes). Uses a computer census with an independent recomputation of each witness.
events.revisions: v2 30 Jul 2026 adds an exhaustive order-14 balance and linear-extension-majority census; the Gold Partition result is unchanged (arXiv comments, per abstract page)
events.delivers: The bullet's window for every finite non-chain poset with at most 14 elements (Corollary 6), and the stronger Gold Partition Conjecture for the same posets (Theorem 5). These are finite instances of the universal claim.
events.remains: Every finite non-chain poset with at least 15 elements; the bullet is open for all larger posets.

machine_checked.system: Author-written exhaustive census program (not a proof assistant); the paper says code and data are archived on Zenodo, and that an independent program, sharing no algorithm with the census, recomputes every extremal witness from its witness string

events.directly_checkable: The extremal witnesses are explicit finite posets, e.g. the ladder with broken rungs attaining 254/725 among posets that are not nontrivial ordinal sums, and the 128 classes attaining 1/3, which are ordinal sums of singletons and copies of one three-element poset. Each can be checked by hand. The full census is not hand-checkable; its code is said to be on Zenodo (not opened).
events.doubts: (1) Single author with no affiliation shown; no peer review. (2) The verification is a computer census whose software the paper says was developed with AI coding tools (see ai). (3) The independent recomputation is the author's own statement; no third party has reproduced it in any source I found. (4) No public engagement in about 11 weeks.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: no counterexample among posets of at most 14 elements, and the lower bound 1/3 holds exactly for these.
events.object: Exhaustive computation over all 1,338,193,159,771 unlabeled posets on 14 elements, with explicit extremal witnesses: the least balance constant above 1/3 is 37/106; exactly 128 classes attain 1/3; the least among posets that are not nontrivial ordinal sums is 254/725, a ladder with broken rungs. The witnesses are explicit; the census is exhaustive, not existential.

systems.name: Anthropic Claude Code (Claude 5 family)
systems.what_it_did: Per the paper, used 'extensively for software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery, and drafting and editing the manuscript'. Claude Code is a coding agent harness, not a bare model. The paper credits it with no mathematical proof step; the software it helped build is the order-14 census that constitutes the verification, so whether this counts as load-bearing is a close call.
systems.basis_quote: Anthropic Claude Code (Claude 5 family) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.6 family) were used extensively for software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery, and drafting and editing the manuscript.

systems.name: OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.6 family)
systems.what_it_did: Per the paper, used in the same sentence and for the same listed purposes as Claude Code: software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery, and manuscript drafting and editing. No proof step is credited to it. Whether the software it helped build is load-bearing is a close call, as for Claude Code.
systems.basis_quote: Anthropic Claude Code (Claude 5 family) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.6 family) were used extensively for software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery, and drafting and editing the manuscript.

events.what_happened: A. Haqi, 'On the Gap of Finite Posets', arXiv 2608.12678 (single author; v1 13 Aug 2026; v2 2 Sep 2026). The abstract page and HTML were read. Studies gap(P), the largest interval missed by the expected ranks h_P(x) = E f(x) of a uniform random order-preserving bijection. Results: a weighted strengthening of an ideal inequality that Kahn conjectured, giving gap(P) <= 2w(P)-1; for any L > 0, a width-two poset whose expected-rank gap is at least L; posets P_r with low-entropy induced orders but gap at least (3/2)^r. Section 2 states the 1/3-2/3 conjecture as delta(P) >= 1/3. Corollary 4.8, which the paper says is 'observed by [AK25, Equation (63)]', states that for finite P with an element incomparable to all others, delta_P(u,v) = 1/2 - o(1) for some distinct u, v as the width grows. The acknowledgements say: 'The key ideas and theorem were found by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol.' and 'The manuscript is written by the author with assistance from Codex.'
events.delivers: The three main results concern gap(P), a quantity built from one-element expected ranks, not delta(P); they say nothing about the bullet's window. Corollary 4.8 gives the bullet's window, indeed nearly 1/2, for large-width posets with a universally incomparable element, and the paper attributes the observation to Aires and Kahn.
events.remains: The bullet in general: posets without a universally incomparable element, and posets of bounded width.
events.directly_checkable: The width-two poset with expected-rank gap at least any prescribed L, and the posets P_r with gap at least (3/2)^r. Both concern gap, not balance; the constructions were not read.
events.doubts: The author's own acknowledgement credits ChatGPT 5.6 Sol with the key ideas and theorem; no human check of the results found. The credited results are about gap, a different quantity from delta(P), and the paper does not say which theorem is meant by 'the theorem' in the acknowledgement.
events.direction: The gap results neither support nor cut against the bullet. Corollary 4.8 is consistent with it.
events.object: (a) A width-two poset whose expected-rank gap is at least any prescribed L > 0. (b) Posets P_r with gap at least (3/2)^r while every selected induced order has low base-two entropy. Both concern gap, not balance; construction types were not established from what I read.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.6 Sol
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, 'the key ideas behind all three results were found by' it (abstract), and the acknowledgement says 'the key ideas and theorem were found by' it. The three results concern gap(P), not the balance constant. Corollary 4.8 is attributed in the text to Aires and Kahn, so the AI credit does not clearly reach the delta(P) statement.
systems.basis_quote: The key ideas behind all three results were found by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol.

events.what_happened: M. Aires, 'Proof of the Kahn-Saks Conjecture', a PDF on the author's USC Dornsife page, dated 25 September 2026 per search excerpts. The PDF could not be read by my tools (binary streams only), so everything below comes from search excerpts of its abstract and introduction. Claims: sufficiently large width forces delta(P), the 'balancing coefficient', to be arbitrarily close to 1/2, answering the Kahn-Saks conjecture; a structural dichotomy for large width (a nearly uniform order on k vertices, or an almost fixed order on t vertices with one further vertex inserted uniformly among the t+1 slots); and, per an excerpt, that the first possibility must occur within any antichain of size Omega(n^(2/3)). arXiv 2609.30888 cites it as '[Air26] Max Aires, Proof of the Kahn-Saks conjecture, in preparation (2026)' and says the conjecture 'was recently resolved by the first author in a companion paper'.
events.delivers: If the claim holds: for every epsilon > 0 there is W such that every finite poset of width at least W has delta(P) >= 1/2 - epsilon. That gives the bullet's window for all finite posets of large width. It does not reach posets of bounded width.
events.remains: Posets of bounded width, and posets of width below W, and the bullet in general.
events.doubts: (1) Single author, self-hosted PDF; no arXiv or journal posting found. (2) Cited by the co-authored paper only as 'in preparation'. (3) The full text was not readable to me, so the argument could not be checked. (4) No independent engagement found. (5) Whether AI was used in it is unknown to me; the co-authored paper's AI statement covers 'the authors', not this companion specifically.
events.direction: If correct, supports the conjecture for large width (delta tends to 1/2 as width grows).

events.what_happened: M. Aires, S. H. Chan, I. Pak and G. Panova, 'Breaking the Infinite Barrier in the 1/3-2/3 Conjecture', arXiv 2609.30888 (posted 25 Sep 2026; v1 only; 45 KB; 31 pages per the comments field; math.CO, cs.DM). The abstract and most of the HTML were read in chunks. Abstract: 'We give an epsilon-improvement for the balance constant over the bound by Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter (1995) for some small epsilon > 0. This is the first general result towards the 1/3-2/3 conjecture in over 30 years.' Theorem 1.2: there is a fixed epsilon > 0 such that for every finite poset that is not a chain there are x, y with (5-sqrt5)/10 + epsilon <= P[f(x) < f(y)] <= (5+sqrt5)/10 - epsilon; the paper calls epsilon 'microscopically small' and the reading tool reported its explicit choice as 3^(-3^(16 x 10^18)), which I did not verify. Theorem 1.4: there is a universal K such that for every finite poset of width greater than K, delta(P) > e^(-1) - 10^(-100); the paper says that since e^(-1) > 1/3 'the result implies the 1/3-2/3 Conjecture in this case'. Section 6.4 takes epsilon = 10^(-100). Section 1.4 says the Kahn-Saks conjecture 'was recently resolved by the first author in a companion paper' [Air26]. AI: the 'Use of AI' section says 'In preparation of the paper, the authors used AI extensively (several different models)', and that AI was used 'for light editing, reference check and various computations', 'in the proofs of several technical lemmas, and as a way to compute the constant in (1.5)', and that 'some computations later needed to be redone by hand'. Section 4.2 says: 'to find the inequalities used in the proof of this lemma, we directed an AI assistant to explore the underlying algebraic optimization problem.' Lemma 4.2 is applied in Section 4.3 to prove Theorem 1.2. The paper names no model.
events.delivers: Theorem 1.2: for every finite non-chain poset, a pair with probability in [0.2764+epsilon, 0.7236-epsilon]. That is a wider window than [1/3, 2/3], so it does not give the bullet. Theorem 1.4: for finite posets of width above K, a pair in the bullet's window, since delta(P) > e^(-1) - 10^(-100) > 1/3, so the bullet holds for those posets.
events.remains: For finite non-chain posets of width at most K, the bullet's window is not established (Theorem 1.2 gives only about 0.2764 plus epsilon); the bullet is open for general finite posets.
events.doubts: (1) The authors state that the AI was used extensively, that AI produced inequalities used in the proof of Lemma 4.2 (which feeds Theorem 1.2), and that some computations later had to be redone by hand; the paper does not identify which steps were redone or how the AI-found inequalities were verified beyond saying they are 'justified explicitly below'. (2) The constant epsilon is microscopically small and was produced partly by AI-assisted computation (per the reading tool, 3^(-3^(16 x 10^18))); I did not verify it. (3) Single version, not refereed, no independent engagement found in 16 days. (4) The title's 'infinite barrier' is the Brightwell-Felsner-Trotter bound, which the authors say is best possible for infinite posets; the theorem is stated for finite posets, so the proof depends on finiteness.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture's direction: a general improvement towards 1/3 that breaks the BFT bound for finite posets, and the bullet's window for finite posets of large width. It does not contradict the infinite counterexample, since the theorem is for finite posets.

disputes.summary: Attribution of the conjecture is inconsistent across sources. Kislitsyn (1968) per the Brightwell 1999 survey (as reported in search excerpts) and the Wikipedia summary; Kislitsyn (1969) per the search excerpt of Brightwell-Felsner-Trotter 1995; Fredman (1975 or 1976) and Linial (1984) credited as independent formulations. The conjecture is named after no single author in the sources I read.

Rozinek's record states both that the approach proves the general 1/3-2/3 conjecture and that 'a more rigorous and detailed proof is still needed'. The two cannot both be the author's settled position; I record the claim and the caveat and do not resolve the conflict.

summary:
The bullet is unsettled as of 11 October 2026, and the record contains a set of events that move parts of it. The strongest recent general event is arXiv 2609.30888 (Aires, Chan, Pak, Panova; posted 25 Sep 2026, single version, unrefereed, no engagement found in 16 days). Its Theorem 1.2 gives a pair in [0.2764+epsilon, 0.7236-epsilon] for every finite non-chain poset; that window is wider than [1/3, 2/3], so the bullet is not established by it, and I record that reading with the authors' own words that it is 'the first general result towards the 1/3-2/3 conjecture in over 30 years'. Its Theorem 1.4 gives delta(P) > e^(-1) - 10^(-100) > 1/3 for finite posets of width above a universal K, which does give the bullet's window for those posets. Anish Gupta's arXiv 2607.23926 (27 Jul 2026, v2 30 Jul) verifies the Gold Partition Conjecture, and so the bullet, for every non-chain poset on at most 14 elements by exhaustive computer census, with explicit witnesses; I treat finite verification as an instance check that moves the universal claim not at all (per section 2 of the instructions), and record the scope. Max Aires's 'Proof of the Kahn-Saks Conjecture' (USC PDF, dated 25 Sep 2026) claims that large width forces delta close to 1/2, which would give the bullet's window for all finite posets of sufficiently large width; I could not read its text, so this rests on search excerpts and on the co-authored paper's citation of it as 'in preparation'. The earlier large-width asymptotics by Aires and Kahn (arXiv 2509.11549, 2510.26134) are restricted to classes and to large n. Haqi's arXiv 2608.12678 (13 Aug 2026) is the AI-credited neighbour: the acknowledgement and abstract credit 'ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' with the key ideas and theorem, but its three theorems concern gap(P), a different quantity; its Corollary 4.8 gives delta close to 1/2 for a restricted class, attributed by the paper to Aires and Kahn.

AI involvement, by event. (a) 2609.30888: the authors say AI was used 'extensively (several different models)', that 'we directed an AI assistant to explore the underlying algebraic optimization problem' to find inequalities used in the proof of Lemma 4.2, which feeds Theorem 1.2, and that 'some computations later needed to be redone by hand'. The paper names no model, so by the naming rule ai.systems is empty; AI involvement is load-bearing per the quoted text, and the later pass must decide how to count unnamed models. (b) 2607.23926: the paper names 'Anthropic Claude Code (Claude 5 family)' and 'OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.6 family)' for software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery and manuscript drafting; it credits no proof step, but the software is the verification, so I record them as systems with a close-call note. (c) 2608.12678: 'ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' is credited with the key ideas of gap results; Codex is credited only with manuscript assistance, so it is not listed as a system. (d) Rozinek (2024) and the Aires companion PDF: no AI statement readable to me, so the AI field is null.

Pre-window work is recorded: Kahn-Saks 1984 (3/11 to 8/11); Linial 1984 and Aigner 1985 for width two (secondary sources only); Brightwell 1989 for semiorders (secondary); Trotter-Gehrlein-Fishburn 1992 for height two; Brightwell-Felsner-Trotter 1995 ((5-sqrt5)/10, optimal for infinite posets); Peczarski 2006 and 2008 (GPC cases); De Loof et al. 2010 (census to 13); Zaguia 2011 and 2016 (N-free; forest cover graphs); Olson-Sagan 2017 (lattices, Young diagrams, some dimension-2 posets); Chen 2017 (family approaching 0.3489); Sah 2018 (width two, 0.33876 except a direct-sum class); Peczarski 2019 (gap conjecture, cited via Gupta); Gaetz-Gao 2020 (Coxeter analogue); Chan-Pak-Panova 2021 and 2023 (cross-product inequalities); Dolores-Cuenca et al. 2024 (lexicographic sums); Rozinek 2024 (claim, caveated). The Harvard-MIT talk of 11 May 2026 by Kahn states the 1/3 conjecture is 'still far' from proof, which is an earlier status point that the September preprints are consistent with.

Close calls, both sides. (i) Whether finite verification through 14 (Gupta) and the large-width asymptotics count for the bullet: per the instructions, finite instances do not move a universal claim, and asymptotic results settle only named classes; I record both and do not classify. (ii) Whether Gupta's AI-assisted software is load-bearing: the paper credits no proof step, and the census is the result; both readings are recorded. (iii) Whether the 2609.30888 AI-found inequalities are load-bearing: the text says they feed Theorem 1.2, so the 'AI assistant' is load-bearing on the paper's own account, but no model is named. (iv) Whether Rozinek's similarity quantity equals delta(P): not established from what I could read. (v) Whether the Wikipedia article (read through a WebFetch summary, not verbatim) now lists the 2026 preprints: the summary says it lists Gupta (2026) and Aires-Chan-Pak-Panova (2026) under known results and says the problem 'remains unsolved'; I could not verify the wikitext verbatim because the curl fetch was blocked pending approval. (vi) The Peczarski gap conjecture's 2019 date is attributed to 2019 by Wikipedia and the Gupta citation; the year the conjecture was first stated is not verified.

Naming note: the key '1-3-2-3-conjecture' is a misnomer for a 1/3-2/3 statement; some search results collided with an unrelated 1-3-2-3 (graph labelling) seminar listing, which I did not research and which is not part of this record.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the record differently: (1) 2609.30888 can be read as settling the bullet's large-width part and as an unrefereed partial improvement elsewhere, with the AI involvement load-bearing and unnamed, so that the bullet is at most partly moved. (2) Gupta's verification could be read as a computer-assisted finite census with the AI-written software as a tool, not as AI doing the mathematics; under that reading, the AI field is empty. (3) Haqi's 'ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' credit could be read as covering all of the paper's results, including Corollary 4.8, if the acknowledgement's 'the theorem' is taken to mean the paper's main theorem about gap; under that reading the AI credit reaches a delta statement, and under the opposite reading it does not. (4) Rozinek's abstract could be read as settling the conjecture, with the author's caveat as boilerplate; the abstract's quantity would then need to be identified with delta(P). (5) The Aires companion PDF could be read as a full resolution of Kahn-Saks, giving the bullet's window for all large-width posets, or as a claim I could not check at all.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The full text of the Aires 'Proof of the Kahn-Saks Conjecture' PDF, its arXiv posting if any, and any expert reading of it. (b) Expert verification of Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 1.2 in arXiv 2609.30888, with the AI-found inequalities checked, and the identity of the 'several different models' that the authors used, if they disclose it. (c) Independent recomputation of Gupta's census from the Zenodo archive, and any engagement with the result. (d) The full text of Rozinek 2024 (IEEE or the Pardubice repository), and a check whether the similarity quantity equals the balance constant delta(P). (e) The full text of Haqi's arXiv 2608.12678, to identify which theorem the acknowledgement's 'the theorem' refers to and whether Corollary 4.8 depends on the AI-credited ideas. (f) The original Kislitsyn 1968, Linial 1984, Brightwell 1989 and Brightwell 1999 texts, to settle the attributions and the exact width-two scope.

incomplete: (1) The Aires Kahn-Saks PDF (dornsife.usc.edu) could not be read; its claim is recorded from search excerpts and from the citation in arXiv 2609.30888. (2) The Rozinek 2024 full text (IEEE Informatics 2024, pp. 532-537) and the Pardubice repository bitstream were blocked; the claim is recorded from the faculty-site record. (3) Brightwell-Felsner-Trotter 1995, Trotter-Gehrlein-Fishburn 1992, Brightwell 1989, Linial 1984, Aigner 1985, Kahn-Saks 1984, Peczarski 2006/2008/2019, De Loof et al. 2010, Chen 2017 (text), Gaetz-Gao 2020 (text), Chan-Pak-Panova 2021 (text), Dolores-Cuenca et al. 2024 (text), Zaguia 2011/2016 (text) and Brightwell 1999 were not read in full; their entries rest on search excerpts, secondary summaries, the arXiv listing, or later papers that cite them, and are marked opened: false where applicable. (4) arXiv 2510.26134 was read at abstract level only; its full text (including any acknowledgements) was not read. (5) arXiv 2609.30888 was read in chunks; the 'Use of AI' text and Section 4.2 were read, but the full bibliography and the remainder of Section 6 were only partly checked. (6) The Gupta Zenodo archive and the independent recomputation were not opened or reproduced. (7) The Wikipedia article was read through a WebFetch summary, not verbatim; its statement that it lists the 2026 preprints under known results could not be checked against the wikitext. (8) The Peczarski gap conjecture's first-stated year is not verified. (9) No check was made that the 2026 papers' authors have posted corrections or replies after 11 October 2026. (10) The 2026 AI-tool statements are quoted from the papers' own text; I did not contact the authors. (11) Several claims in search excerpts (for example the Aires companion's 'antichain of size Omega(n^(2/3))' bound) were not verified in the full text.
